name: Buflomedil mesotherapy

lead: Buflomedil is a vasoactive drug originally used for leg pain from poor circulation. In mesotherapy, small injections into or just under the skin, it has been used in mixtures meant to improve blood flow to the treated area.

The appearance logic claimed for hair use is that better local circulation could support the scalp and follicles. The published human work found in this area is on body contouring and on the drug's circulatory uses, not on hair.

paras: Mesotherapy is done by a practitioner with shallow injections of a drug mix into the skin. Buflomedil has been one ingredient in some mixes. Specific protocols are not described here.

The European Medicines Agency told doctors to stop prescribing buflomedil in November 2011 over severe neurological and cardiac toxicity, and the European Commission advised revoking its authorizations. The FDA has not approved it. Mesotherapy itself has been linked to infections in some reports.

chain: Injected locally via mesotherapy it is meant to raise blood flow in the treated skin
Better-supplied follicles, as proponents of the approach suggest
angle.text: People who use buflomedil in mesotherapy do so on the idea that local vasodilation could support hair-bearing skin. This mechanism is a claim and has not been tested for hair in the studies reviewed.

lead: Buflomedil (brand name Loftyl) is a vasoactive drug used for claudication, the leg pain of peripheral arterial disease, acting as an alpha-1 and alpha-2 adrenergic antagonist and weak calcium channel blocker [1]. It was suspended in the European Union in 2011 over severe neurological and cardiac toxicity, and the FDA has not approved it [1].

Mesotherapy is a technique in which vitamins, plant extracts, enzymes or drugs are delivered into the skin by shallow or subcutaneous injection; it was founded by French physician Michel Pistor and is best known cosmetically for fat reduction [2]. Buflomedil appears in a published mesotherapy mixture for body contouring [3].

Its place in hair mesotherapy rests on the vasodilation concept: improving circulation to the scalp. No hair trial of buflomedil appears among published studies that were reviewed, while its use in circulatory disease has been examined in Cochrane reviews [4][5].

paras: Buflomedil is a non-selective antagonist of alpha-1 and alpha-2 adrenergic receptors and a weak calcium channel blocker [1].

On 17 November 2011 the European Medicines Agency advised doctors to stop prescribing it over severe neurological and cardiac toxicity, and the European Commission advised member states to revoke its marketing authorization [1].

Mesotherapy delivers substances into the skin through shallow injections [2]. It has no proven clinical efficacy for cosmetic purposes according to Wikipedia, and infections after treatment have been reported in Australia [2].

A 12-week study of 20 women injected a mix of aminophylline, buflomedil and lidocaine into the dermis for body contouring [3]. Cochrane reviews have examined buflomedil for acute ischaemic stroke and intermittent claudication [4][5]. No studies of buflomedil for hair were found.

timeline.event: Randomized study of a mesotherapy mix containing buflomedil for body contouring is published [3].
EMA tells doctors to stop prescribing buflomedil; EU authorizations revoked on advice of the Commission [1].
